<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="PubMed-not-MEDLINE" Owner="NLM"><PMID Version="1">33015623</PMID><DateRevised><Year>2024</Year><Month>08</Month><Day>11</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Print-Electronic"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Electronic">2632-7376</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Internet"><Volume>1</Volume><Issue>1</Issue><PubDate><Year>2020</Year></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Cerebral cortex communications</Title><ISOAbbreviation>Cereb Cortex Commun</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>Sharp Wave-Ripples in Human Amygdala and Their Coordination with Hippocampus during NREM Sleep.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>tgaa051</StartPage><MedlinePgn>tgaa051</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">tgaa051</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1093/texcom/tgaa051</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Cooperative interactions between the amygdala and hippocampus are widely regarded as critical for overnight emotional processing of waking experiences, but direct support from the human brain for such a dialog is absent. Using overnight intracranial recordings in 4 presurgical epilepsy patients (3 female), we discovered ripples within human amygdala during nonrapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, a brain state known to contribute to affective processing. Like hippocampal ripples, amygdala ripples are associated with sharp waves, linked to sleep spindles, and tend to co-occur with their hippocampal counterparts. Moreover, sharp waves and ripples are temporally linked across the 2 brain structures, with amygdala ripples occurring during hippocampal sharp waves and <i>vice versa</i>. Combined with further evidence of interregional sharp-wave and spindle synchronization, these findings offer a potential physiological substrate for the NREM-sleep-dependent consolidation and regulation of emotional experiences.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>&#xa9; The Author(s) 2020.
